fatal_errors: The proposed intervention does not reconstruct the controlled Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr composition series in BCC HfNbTaTiZr or its Hf-balanced equimolar baseline.
It substitutes creep and nanoindentation at at least 1000 °C for the target tensile-strength, modulus, elongation, fracture, and thermal-expansion tests conducted mainly at 300 K and up to 1200 K.
No explicit thermoelastic observable or quantitative prediction is given, so the claimed thermoelastic mechanism cannot be cleanly evaluated.

The cited evidence supports lattice-strain-associated dislocation behavior or irradiation-induced distortion, but not the asserted high-temperature causal link to creep resistance and thermoelastic response.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses refractory HEAs, lattice strain, dislocations, and high-temperature behavior, so it is a scientifically plausible alternative. It nevertheless has little agreement with the hidden study: it omits the HfNbTaTiZr composition sweep, MEAM molecular dynamics, equimolar reference values, nonmonotonic composition dependence, temperature-driven loss of tensile strength and modulus, reduced thermal expansion in selected compositions, and shear-associated ductile fracture. The heterogeneous-versus-homogeneous comparison and null-result falsification rule provide some discriminability, but the baseline is not operationally defined and composition or processing changes used to alter lattice strain would introduce confounders. Neutron diffraction can measure average or phase-resolved lattice strain and defect-related peak changes, but it generally cannot directly resolve individual kink, jog, or cross-slip events; post-test TEM would provide only indirect temporal attribution. Thus the proposal is novel and testable in broad terms, but it is neither a reconstruction of the target nor adequately evidenced for its full creep–thermoelastic causal chain.
